## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):

  hotel YC-L features.

- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.

- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Right after I've said how it fits today's way, asking what it does better than that way is the obvious next thing to pin down before strangers see the solution.
screens.why2: Plain question and hint; 'one benefit a line, up to four, each up to 9 words' tells me exactly how to type it, and the 'what reservation agents would get' phrasing is my trade's people.
screens.why3: As the founder I know what Codyco gives the desk over their callback list: missed calls become bookings and callers get answered when the desk is busy.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape 'I'm not sure', which fits a typed box and leaves the dimension out as the card says.
screens.why5: Nothing is rewritten here; my two benefits stand as typed for Keel to check on the next screen.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 equal benefits of at most 9 words, each a change against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape, exactly the card's founder shape; my two rows are distinct noun phrases and the lead one is a row.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Codyco does better than today's way, checking Keel's draft of my benefits is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Missed calls, bookings and a busy desk are everyday words for any reservation agent or revenue director in a German hotel group.
screens.why3: Every reservation agent sees the missed-call list and knows whether those callers ended up booking, so the benefits are things they live with daily.
screens.why4: The two rows overlap: answering callers when the desk is busy is mostly how missed calls get turned into bookings, so they are close to one gain split in two.
screens.why5: "Missed calls turned into bookings" is my line, but "when the desk is busy" narrows my after hours, peak and holidays to peak alone, dropping the nights and Sundays that make up most of my 5%.
screens.why7: The belief carries both benefits in order and the bar is right, but its occasion is "their last booking call" instead of the missed one, a call answered fine that no benefit can be true of, and the two rows overlap.
screens.instead: Rows: Missed booking calls turned into bookings · Calls answered after hours, at peak and on holidays; Keel will test: For most, with it, their last shift with a missed call would have given them missed booking calls turned into bookings and calls answered after hours, at peak and on holidays.

screens.why1: Right after I've said what it does better, asking what my reservation agents have to do to start using it is the obvious next question in the solution step.
screens.why2: "What will they have to do to start using it?" with "setup, extra steps or learning" is plain to me as a founder selling to reservation offices, and the 9-word limit is clear.
screens.why3: I know what my pilots ask of the desk: forwarding the missed booking calls to Codyco and picking up the calls the AI hands back, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: The only option is the box plus the *I'm not sure* chip, and that escape fits, because a founder who doesn't know the effort should be able to leave the dimension out.
screens.why5: My two efforts went in as I'd say them, handing the missed booking calls to the AI and taking every call it hands to the desk, and the screen adds nothing that changes them.
screens.why7: The screen asks for 1 to 4 efforts of at most 9 words, with the *I'm not sure* escape, and my two rows are base-form steps the agents take themselves in *their* voice (one handover habit, one new habit of use); the hint doesn't say *themselves*, but nothing here bends a rule.
screens.instead: What will reservation agents themselves have to do to start using it (not their director, IT or your team)? Up to four, each up to 9 words · I'm not sure

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, Keel shows back the steps it drew from that, which is where this check belongs, though the title repeating as the intro's first line and 'Solution · 4 of 4' beside 'Step 3 of 4' read a little clumsily.
screens.why2: 'Missed booking calls', 'the desk' and an AI handing a call over are how my reservation agents and I talk about the shift; nothing needs a second read.
screens.why3: Both are things a reservation agent does with their own hands: letting the rung-out calls go to Codyco, and picking up the ones it passes back to the desk.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, the letting-go and the new habit of taking handovers, each under 9 words in the trade's words, with no Keel suggestion added and nothing missing that I'd test here.
screens.why5: These are the two rows I kept from revisions 24 and 25 word for word, saved as drafted, and they still mean what I typed.
screens.why7: Each row is one effort on the one measure, in 'their' voice, a step the agent takes themselves (not IT's forwarding setup, which Compatibility tests, nor the director's sign-off, which Purchase friction tests), 2 rows within 1 to 4, so either answer could support or refute 'Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI'.

screens.why1: After writing the efforts my agents face, picking the one most likely to stop them is the obvious next step before Keel tests it.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls, the AI and the desk are words my reservation agents and I use every shift, and the title is a one-read question.
screens.why3: Both rows are things an agent decides about their own phone line and their own desk, so I can choose from what I know of my customers.
screens.why4: The two rows are my own: one is giving the missed calls up to the AI, the other is the new habit of taking its handovers. They are distinct, and nothing is missing or odd.
screens.why5: Both rows are what I typed, unchanged as the intro promises, and the belief repeats my picked row word for word.
screens.why7: Both are steps the agent takes themselves (letting the AI have the missed calls, taking its handovers), in 'their' voice and under 9 words. Neither is Compatibility's forwarding or Purchase friction's review, and the Yes/Only if/Probably not/No item with the 1-in-3 bar can both hold and fail on the pick.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the right place to decide whether to collect pilot leads, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is my own word (my Zero Risk Pilot), and the hint shows the exact line people will see, so I can answer at first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from the people who answer is my own call to make.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice, the two options are distinct, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid, money-back €3,000 pilot at one hotel that the director signs off, but the line "Would you try this for real? Leave your email." reads like a free trial for whoever answers, usually a reservation agent who cannot sign for it.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "We run a money-back pilot at one hotel. Want us to reach whoever decides on it at your group? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking who asks my questions belongs right before the link goes out to reservation agents, after the pilot offer and before launch.
screens.why2: Two names with a five-second sample and a plain hint about video, typing or tapping, and a flat 400 credits are clear on first read.
screens.why3: I can judge which voice my German reservation agents would sit through by hearing both samples myself.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct and playable, but neither chip says what language or accent it speaks, which is the one thing I need for agents in Germany; the hint also says 'voice' while the interviewer is on video, and my own pick was about a face.
screens.why5: Nothing about Codyco, the AI receptionist or the director leaks into this choice, and my study's actor, reservation agents, is kept.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions? Daphne (English) ▶ 5 s · Saskia (German) ▶ 5 s, with a line saying the questions are asked and written in German for agents in DE.

screens.why1: After picking who asks the questions, choosing how the reservation agents will answer is the obvious next step before sending the link.
screens.why2: The three options are plain; 'AI interviewer · Daphne' is explained in the same line, and I build AI voice agents so the idea is familiar to me.
screens.why3: I know reservation agents work at a desk or in a central office between calls, so I can judge whether they would read and tap or talk to a video interviewer.
screens.why4: Video AI, text, or let them pick covers the real choices, the options are distinct, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It is a delivery setting that does not touch my idea's words, and nothing of Codyco leaks into it.

screens.why1: After choosing how agents answer, deciding who gets the link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; "Contacts page" is Keel's own screen, and "signs in with Google" is clear to me.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to reservation agents I know by name from our pilot hotels and the groups we work with.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people (named contacts, a Keel search list, an open group link) are distinct and complete, and no escape is needed for a choice about my own sending.
screens.why5: It is about how I send the study, nothing of my product or roles is changed or shown to respondents.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right under the title, and the tally "3 beliefs: 3 holding · 7 people answered" is beside it, with each card's count against its bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what was counted (said yes, would have gone better, would do it), over 7 people, against a bar of 5 of 7, so all three read at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction are my dimensions and the forwarding and handover lines are mine, but the solution statement is garbled ("the hotel's reservation desk the hotel forwards the call", the confirmed booking in the PMS said twice) and the advantage line ("their last booking call would have given them missed calls turned into bookings") is mangled wording of my belief.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for Codyco, such as going ahead with the pilot pitch or firming up relative advantage, which sits exactly on the bar; the only closing line explains how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible and "at the bar" is flagged, but a clean "Holding up" on 7 agents, with relative advantage at exactly 5 of 7 and 3 of 6 adopting only on a condition, is never called thin or borderline.
screens.instead: Holding up on 7 agents, but thin: relative advantage only just reaches the bar (5 of 7) and half of those who would hand calls to the AI set a condition, so ask more agents and read those conditions before leaning on this in the pilot pitch.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Holding up* sits right beside *6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7*, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bars show what was counted (could they forward), the strip shows 7 people with the marker at 5, and the for and against split (6 to 1) is plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and *Most reservation agents could forward unanswered calls to another number* are my row as I checked it, although the bar line *You said could forward...* drops its subject and reads broken.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that call forwarding is not my blocker and sends me to Adoption friction next, which is where I would look anyway.
screens.why_b5: The count line says *a lean, not a call*, but the So line then states flatly that forwarding *is not what will stop them* and that Adoption friction *is*, which is more than 7 agents can carry, and it passes over Aylin's old phone system that cannot forward without IT and an owner who won't pay.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean: 6 of 7 could forward their unanswered calls, but one agent's old phone system can't forward without IT and the owner's money, so have a fallback ready for old systems, then look at Adoption friction.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 for, bar 5 of 7, at the bar, so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The bar and the 7 are plain, but Better 5 5 a lot 0 a little took me a second read to see it as 5 better, all 5 a lot.
screens.why_b3: Both my benefits are in the belief, but the occasion reads last booking call and the question asks about any shift with booking calls, not the shift with a missed call I set, and the bar line quotes only my first benefit.
screens.why_b4: Pointing me to Adoption friction is useful, but it does not tell me what to do with the two against, Chiara's call center already covering after hours and Tobias refusing to hand guests to a machine.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, it says a lean, not a call, and that it is a hypothetical, so nothing overclaims a result sitting exactly on the bar.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 said a lot better, on the bar, so one more no would flip it; the two against are a group whose call center already answers after hours and a desk that wants a person, so check whether groups with a call center are your buyer.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, and with only Tobias against, the 1-in-3 rule plainly passes, so I know it held and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over the 7 agents, split for and against, and the strip's marker at 5 against 6 for cells shows where the bar sits on first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI' are the step I picked, though 'You said hand their missed booking calls to the AI' reads clumsily.
screens.why_b4: The So line points 'below' for what would make it worth it, but the condition is already on the screen (answers in the hotel's voice, all three the same), and it never tells me to make that the thing my €3,000 pilot proves at the first hotel.
screens.why_b5: n stays at 7 throughout, the conditional half is split out rather than folded into a strong yes, and it says plainly this is a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Holding up, 6 of 7 (3 only if it answers in the hotel's voice, the same condition each time): make the hotel's own voice and name what the pilot shows first, and ask the one No, Tobias, what would change his mind.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Holding up' with its deciding count beside it (6 of 7 against a bar of 5; 5 of 7 at the bar of 5), and the summary line repeats the verdict with the number.
screens.why_b3: The Compatibility belief is the forwarding line I checked, but the Relative advantage belief reads as a garbled template ('their last booking call would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') that I recognise but would never have written.
screens.why_b4: Neither box says what the dissent means for the idea, e.g. that old phone systems need an IT or hardware path before a pilot, or that groups whose call center already covers after hours are a weaker fit.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible, but 'the 1 who said no' and 'the 2 who said no' recast 'Only sometimes', 'Worse' and 'No difference' as plain no's, and a 5-of-7 result sitting exactly on the bar is called held with no word that n is 7 or that it is a bare pass.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: the owner won't pay to replace a phone system that can only ring the desk, some guests call precisely to reach a person who knows the house, and where a call center already covers after six the real pain moves to group emails without rates.
screens.instead: Compatibility held 6 of 7, but one hotel's phones can only ring the desk and the owner won't pay to replace them, so check the phone system before you sell the pilot; Relative advantage just made the bar (5 of 7): one agent won't hand guests to a machine, and one group's call center already covers after six, so lead with groups that have no after-hours cover.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it plainly checks whether I'm in the right place, at a German hotel group with a central reservations office, before anything else is asked.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call centre are the words we use at work, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why3: I know where I work and that our group runs a central reservations office in Munich, so this is about my own job.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it completely for a screener, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, hotel groups in Germany with a central reservations office or call centre, and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: The question says well in one breath, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky for a yes-or-no and is not the screener form the amendment sets, which is the stem and then 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you work at a hotel group in Germany that runs a central reservations office or call centre? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I work in a central reservations office, asking whether I had a recent shift with calls is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words; I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether calls came in on my shift, I take dozens every shift.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, but No is true of nobody who worked a shift, so in practice there's only one answer for me.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but the founder's problem was calls that don't get answered, and this only asks whether calls came in, so the problem dropped out.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Yes or no' is easy to hold and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance every reservation agent is in (calls came in), not the costly event (a booking call went unanswered), so everyone says Yes, No has no one and the belief can never be refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered? Yes · No

screens.why1: After the screen check and whether a booking call came in this week, this is the natural point to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Missed calls, the payment, the confirmed booking and the PMS are all everyday words at our reservations desk, so I follow it on the first read.
screens.why3: Calls nobody picks up on a trade-fair Saturday are exactly what I live with, so I can picture this against my own shifts.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: It reads as a deliberate idea card and keeps the founder's point of turning unanswered booking calls into bookings, though *your hotel* sits a little oddly for someone in a group's central office.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is a long run of six sentences with *answers ... answers* back to back and *by rules your hotel sets* tacked on the end, which I would only half hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI that answers the booking calls nobody picks up: it takes the guest's questions and payment, puts the booking straight into your PMS, and passes calls to your reservations office by your own rules; the people building it believe it would turn missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card about an AI that answers missed calls, asking whether our missed calls could even be sent somewhere else is the obvious first thing to check.
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, but pinning *forwarded unanswered calls* to *your last booking call* needs a second read, since I answered that call, so it wasn't unanswered.
screens.why3: In our central office the overflow and forwarding rules sit in the ACD and are set by IT or the telephony admin, not by me at the desk, so I would partly be guessing what they would allow.
screens.why4: My true answer is *only IT or my team lead could set that up*, which isn't on the list, and *Yes, most of the time* and *Only sometimes* read oddly about a single call.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose and the question stays on the founder's step of getting missed calls to another number, in words my trade uses.
screens.why6: It is short, asks one question, and the four options plus *you can't tell* are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The condition is served as an ability, but for an agent forwarding is a permission held by IT, so the ability rungs bend the kind; the measure, order, balance and escape otherwise meet the card.
screens.instead: Think of your last booking shift. Could unanswered calls have been forwarded to another number? Yes, easily · Yes, with some steps · Only with help or approval · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the forwarding question, asking whether Codyco would have helped on my shift is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: "Have done that better" leaves me guessing what *that* is, since the stem names calls coming in rather than anything I did, so I need a second read to work out what I am judging.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last Saturday shift went, which calls I got to and which rang out.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it with no overlap, and I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Calling the product an "AI reservation agent" gives it my own job title, which reads like the founder's pitch term and lands oddly when I am the reservation agent.
screens.why6: The stem runs well past 20 words with the idea's long name in the middle, so by the time it reaches "or not" I have nearly lost what was asked, though the four options say well.
screens.why7: The four fixed options and the escape are right, but the occasion is any shift with calls rather than the missed-call case the advantage is for, which the card lists as a pitfall.
screens.instead: Think of the last call on your shift that nobody picked up. Would Codyco have handled it better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea and whether it would do better, asking whether I'd actually take it on is the obvious last question of this part.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls and handing them over are how we talk on a busy trade-fair Saturday, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: Whether missed calls go to an overflow line is set in the phone system by our office lead or IT, not by me at my headset, so I'd partly be guessing about my own say in it.
screens.why4: Yes, a real condition about sounding like our hotel, probably not and no are distinct and complete, and I can't tell fits as the one escape.
screens.why5: It uses the idea card's own words, shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan leaks in.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold, then the escape, with nothing that only the eye can read.
screens.why7: The condition is a fair assurance and the shape, balance and escape are right, but handing over missed calls is mostly a routing decision the office makes and barely an effort of mine, so the measure leans to whether I'd accept it rather than what using it costs me.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd check the bookings it took while you were on other calls and fix any wrong ones yourself. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it flags the ones it wasn't sure of · Probably not · No · I can't tell
